verdict.rationale: Both refactors look behavior-preserving on inspection, and both give a named state enum, one function per token kind, and a single place that handles errors. B fits the user's two hard constraints better. Its permanent exhaustive equivalence test against a frozen copy of the old tokenizer covers a multi-byte character, and its benchmark (min over 100 interleaved rounds) found that inlining mattered, which it documents. A's structure is somewhat cleaner and its seven targeted tests are good. However, A dropped its equivalence harness and has no guard against a slowdown from inlining in the method-split design.
a_issues: Deleted the old-vs-new equivalence harness after using it. Only seven example tests are left to guard a refactor whose main requirement is identical output.
The speed check is weak: 5 rounds where the noise is larger than any difference. Nothing ensures the split helpers get inlined on the hot path.
The comparison alphabet had no multi-byte character, so the UTF-8 slicing boundaries were not exercised.
b_issues: Adds a 159-line frozen copy of the old tokenizer under tests/. It must be edited by hand every time the format changes on purpose, which is the scenario the user is preparing for.
The exhaustive test covers about 11 million strings. The report gives 1.5 s in release, but plain `cargo test` runs in debug and will likely be much slower.
`#[inline(always)]` on every helper adds noise. The second `impl Tokens` block is placed after the Iterator impl, which makes the file layout a bit scattered.

verdict.rationale: Both refactors preserve the original tokens, errors and positions, and both reports describe exhaustive old-versus-new comparisons and release-build benchmarks. B is cleaner: it applies the stop-after-error rule once in `next()`, and its scanners carry no `#[inline(always)]` boilerplate. It also adds focused, readable regression tests for the edge cases the existing tests missed. A's equivalence harness gives strong refactor protection, but it commits a 159-line frozen copy of the old tokenizer that must be updated whenever the format changes. That reintroduces the maintenance burden the user wanted to get rid of.
a_issues: Commits a full frozen copy of the old monolithic tokenizer (`tests/support/reference.rs`) as a permanent second implementation that must be updated whenever the format changes.
Every helper is marked `#[inline(always)]`, and the report says removing these makes it 30% slower. This adds noise and a fragile performance dependency.
Adds no targeted regression tests that document individual edge cases; it relies on the brute-force comparison alone.
b_issues: The exhaustive old-versus-new comparison was deleted after use, so the equivalence claim cannot be re-checked from the PR.
No inlining hints; the speed relies on the compiler's default inlining. B's benchmark shows parity, but this is less guarded than A's explicit hints.
The `Nothing` state is also documented as 'line exhausted', but `next()` does not set it when the line ends (only on error). This is a minor doc inaccuracy.
